title: Nest type transitions as key innovations in the Furnariidae (Aves: Passeriformes)
content:
Abstract
Studies on key innovations aim to understand how the emergence of a trait permits transitions to new ecological niches. Passerine nest shifts have been shown to be key innovations for the exploitation of new temperature niches, but their relationships with other important niche dimensions remain obscure. Here, we addressed the hypothesis of nest type transitions as key innovations for two important proxies of niche diversification, foraging substrate and habitat, across the genera of one of the biggest passerine radiations, the Neotropical Furnariidae. Ancestral state reconstructions evidenced the common ancestor of the group nesting within tree cavities in forests and foraging in bark (tree trunks). Shifts in nest type were correlated with shifts in foraging substrate. Although burrow nesting emerged before ground foraging, being a potential key innovation for this foraging substrate, bark foraging was a constraint for nest type diversification, and the type of correlation between enclosed nesting and vegetation substrate was equivocal. Correlations with habitat were mixed, with enclosed nesting preceding shifts to non-forest habitats. We show that nest type diversification can be a key innovation for shifts in foraging substrate and habitat, opening new sources of investigations on avian evolution, but in the furnariids it depended on nest type and lineage.
